title: Switching Fundamentals
tagline: How frames move inside a broadcast domain.
summary: A switch is a self-learning forwarding engine. This module covers frames, MAC learning, flooding, VLANs and trunks, and why loops are catastrophic without STP.
objectives: Describe the Ethernet frame fields that matter for switching decisions.
Explain MAC learning and the three possible forwarding decisions for any frame.
Predict what a switch does with unknown unicast, broadcast and known unicast traffic.
Explain access ports, trunk ports and 802.1Q tagging, including the native VLAN trap.
Explain why a loop breaks a network and what STP actually does about it.
key_questions: How does a switch build its MAC address table?
When does a switch flood a frame, and when does it filter?
What breaks when two switches are connected twice with no STP?

assessment.prompt: A switch receives a frame with an unknown destination MAC. What does it do with it?
options: Sends it back out the port it arrived on
Sends it to the default gateway
Floods it out every port in the same VLAN except the ingress port
assessment.explanation: Unknown unicast is flooded within the VLAN/broadcast domain so the destination has a chance to answer and teach the switch its location. Flooding never includes the ingress port.

why_wrong.3: Dropping would make the first frame of every conversation fail.
why_wrong.0: Sending back out the ingress port is never correct for a switch.
why_wrong.1: Switches do not have a default gateway; that is a Layer 3 concept.

assessment.prompt: Two PCs are on access ports in VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 of the same switch. What is required for them to communicate?
options: A Layer 3 device or an SVI/router-on-a-stick to route between the VLANs
Nothing, the switch forwards between VLANs automatically
A trunk between the two access ports
STP must elect the switch as root
assessment.explanation: VLANs are separate broadcast domains and therefore separate subnets. Moving between them is routing, which needs a Layer 3 interface in each VLAN (SVI) or a router with subinterfaces.

why_wrong.1: A switch does not forward between VLANs by default.
why_wrong.2: A trunk carries multiple VLANs to another switch or router, it does not make two access ports routable.
why_wrong.3: STP prevents loops; it has nothing to do with inter-VLAN routing.

assessment.prompt: Explain, step by step, how a switch learns where MAC address aa:bb:cc:00:11:22 lives, and how that knowledge is used afterwards.

checklist.text: The switch records the source MAC of every received frame together with the ingress port.
The entry is refreshed each time the source MAC is seen; it ages out after a timeout (typically 300s).
For a known destination MAC, the frame is forwarded only out the mapped port (filter/forward).
If the destination is unknown, the frame is flooded within the VLAN.
If the destination is on the ingress port, the frame is filtered (dropped) because the device already has it.

assessment.reference: Learning is entirely passive and based on source addresses. Every frame that arrives teaches the switch 'this MAC is behind this port'. Entries live in the MAC address table (CAM table) and age out after a few minutes of silence. Forwarding uses the destination address: known destination means forward out exactly one port; unknown means flood inside the VLAN; destination on the ingress port means filter. A MAC appearing on a different port causes the table to move the entry — which is normal when a device is moved, and a symptom of a loop when it flaps constantly.
